theme: Make a joyful noise, all the earth
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 100. You read it earlier in the Gospel of John. Read it now as the closing call of the missionary psalms: all the earth is invited to enter his gates with thanksgiving.
settingTheScene: Psalm 100 completes a cluster of psalms (93 to 100) that celebrate the kingship of the LORD. It is the last and most compact of the invitations to all the earth. Having read psalms about declaring his glory and salvation to the nations, we come to the response: what the nations do when they come. They come to worship with gladness and gratitude.
observation: “Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth!” (v. 1).
“Know that the LORD, he is God!” (v. 3).
“It is he who made us, and we are his” (v. 3).
“We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (v. 3).
“Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise!” (v. 4).
“Give thanks to him; bless his name!” (v. 4).
“For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations” (v. 5).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with an invitation to “all the earth.” The audience is the same as in Psalm 96 and 98. Here the focus is on the response of those who have heard the news and believed. They come with a joyful noise.

Verse 3 gives the basis for a right relationship: “Know that the LORD, he is God!” Knowing who God is comes first. The nations who once worshiped idols are now taught to know the LORD. “It is he who made us, and we are his.” This is the confession of every convert. We belong to the one who made us. We are his people, the sheep of his pasture, the language of the shepherd. In Acts, the Gentiles who believe are included in this: “those who are far off” have been brought near (Ephesians 2:13), and they are now part of God’s flock.

The call to enter his gates with thanksgiving shows the approach. We come to God not because we deserve it but with gratitude. Thanksgiving is the doorway. In Psalm 100, there is no sacrifice for sin mentioned, no priest, only joy. Under the new covenant, this joy rests on the finished sacrifice of Christ. We can enter the courts with praise because the way is open.

The final verse gives the threefold reason: the LORD is good (his character), his steadfast love endures forever (his covenant commitment), and his faithfulness extends to all generations (his reliability). Paul and the apostles saw this in action: the generations of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and David, and now the church. God has been faithful across the centuries, and he is faithful now.

Notice how the invitation and the response connect Acts to the Psalms. The command to the nations is the mission of the church. The response of the nations is the church’s worship. In every city, from Antioch to Ephesus, new congregations were formed, singing, giving thanks, and calling on the name of the Lord. Psalm 100 is the picture of their gatherings.
connection: Psalm 95 begins in a similar way. Psalm 117 is the shortest invitation to the nations. Ezekiel 34:30-31 calls Israel the flock of God. John 10:14-16 speaks of one flock, one shepherd. Ephesians 2:11-22 describes Gentiles brought near. Colossians 3:16-17 speaks of singing with thankfulness in your hearts. Hebrews 12:28 calls for acceptable worship with reverence and awe. Revelation 7:9-12 pictures the nations worshiping.
application:
Begin worship this week with thanksgiving. Enter his gates with a list of at least five things you are grateful for.

Read the psalm to someone who is new to the faith.

Thank God for the generations of faithful people who passed the gospel down to you.
prayerPrompts: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, naming why.
Thank him that he made you and you are his.
